---
title: "Reading a Push Button"
unit: 3
cluster: "Reading Sensors"
---

A program often has to wait for a person to tell it something: start, stop,
or next. To let it read a push button, we connect the button to an **input
pin**, and the program reads the pin to see whether the button is pressed.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

- connect the button to a pin of the board
- read the button from the REPL
- light the LED from a program while the button is pressed
- slow down a blinking LED with the button

## Connecting the button to the board

The button stays in the same holes, `d34`, `d36`, `g34` and `g36`. This
time, it connects a pin of the board to GND, and the LED goes back on D15.
Unplug the USB cable. Then:

1. Take out the blue jumper wire from `a34` to `a23`, and the red jumper
   wire from `a36` to the `+` rail.
2. Put the yellow jumper wire back, from `a7`, below D15, to `a23`.
3. Connect `a36` to the `−` rail with a black jumper wire. This connects one
   side of the button to GND.
4. Connect `j9`, above D7, to `j34` with a jumper wire. This connects GPIO7
   to the other side. The wire uses the top half of column 34, so that it
   does not cross the yellow wire: `j34` is joined to `a34` through the
   button's pins.

![The LED circuit from D15, on a full-length breadboard, with a push button straddling the centre gap in `d34`, `d36`, `g34` and `g36`. A jumper wire connects D7 to `j34`, and a black jumper wire connects `a36` to the `−` rail. Board photo: PCBCupid.](../images/glyph-c6-breadboard-button-d7.svg)

Pressing the button connects GPIO7 to GND. Releasing it leaves GPIO7
connected to nothing at all.

## Reading the button

Plug in the USB cable, connect Thonny to the board, and set up GPIO7 as an
input in the REPL:

```session
>>> from machine import Pin
```

```session
>>> button = Pin(7, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
```

`Pin.IN` sets up GPIO7 as an **input**, so the program can read it.

`Pin.PULL_UP` matters here. A pin that is connected to nothing does not read
as off: it picks up stray electricity from the air and from our hands, and
reads 0 or 1 at random. This is called a **floating** pin. `Pin.PULL_UP`
connects the pin to 3.3 volts inside the chip, through a resistor, so it
reads 1 when nothing else is connected. When the button connects the pin to
GND, GND wins, because the resistor lets only a little current through, and
the pin reads 0.

Read the pin without touching the button:

```session
>>> button.value()
```

`value()` returns 1. Now hold the button down, and read the pin again:

```session
>>> button.value()
```

This time it returns 0. With a pull-up, the values are the other way round
from what we might expect: **1 means released, and 0 means pressed**.

::: {.callout-warning}
Without `Pin.PULL_UP`, the program still runs and gives no error. The pin
reads 0 when the button is pressed, but when it is released it reads 0 or 1
at random, so the program sees presses that never happened.
:::

## Lighting the LED from a program

To light the LED while the button is held down, a program reads the button
over and over, and turns the LED on or off to match. Type this program in
the editor:

```python
from machine import Pin

led = Pin(15, Pin.OUT)
button = Pin(7, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)

while True:
    if button.value() == 0:
        led.on()
    else:
        led.off()
```

`button.value() == 0` is true while the button is pressed. The loop has no
`sleep`: it checks the button thousands of times a second, so the LED
follows the button as soon as we press or release it.

Click Run. The LED is off. Hold the button down, and the LED lights; let go,
and it goes off. Click Stop to end the program.

The LED does what it did with the button wired straight into its circuit.
The difference is that the program now decides: change `== 0` to `== 1`,
and the same button turns the LED off instead.

## Changing the blink speed

Since the program decides what a press does, a press can do something other
than light the LED. Here, each press makes the LED blink more slowly. Type
this program in the editor:

```python
from machine import Pin
import time

led = Pin(15, Pin.OUT)
button = Pin(7, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)

delay = 0.1

while True:
    if button.value() == 0:
        delay = delay + 0.1
        print(delay)
        while button.value() == 0:
            time.sleep(0.01)
    else:
        led.on()
        time.sleep(delay)
        led.off()
        time.sleep(delay)
```

`delay` is how long the LED stays on, and then off, in seconds. Each time
round the loop, the program checks the button once:

- If the button is released, it blinks the LED once, with the current
  `delay`.
- If the button is pressed, it adds 0.1 to `delay`, prints the new value in
  the Shell, and waits until the button is released.

The inner `while` loop does the waiting: it keeps sleeping for a hundredth
of a second for as long as the button reads 0. Without it, the outer loop
would come back to the check a moment later, while the button is still
down, and add 0.1 again and again for as long as we hold it. With it, one
press adds 0.1 once, however long we hold the button.

Click Run. The LED blinks fast. Press the button, and the Shell shows the
new delay, and the LED blinks a little more slowly. Each press slows it
down further. Click Stop to end the program; running it again starts from
0.1 seconds.

::: {.callout-note}
The program checks the button only between blinks. While it is in
`time.sleep(delay)`, it does not look at the button, so a quick press can be
missed. Hold the button until the Shell shows the new delay. The slower the
LED blinks, the longer we have to hold it.
:::

## Summary

A program reads a push button through an input pin with a pull-up, which
reads 1 while the button is released and 0 while it is pressed.

| Connection or code | What it does |
|--------------------|--------------|
| GPIO pin and GND on the two sides of the button | pressing the button connects the pin to GND |
| `button = Pin(7, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)` | sets up GPIO7 as an input, pulled up to 3.3 volts inside the chip |
| `button.value()` | returns 1 while the button is released, and 0 while it is pressed |
| An input pin connected to nothing | floats: it reads 0 or 1 at random |
| `if button.value() == 0:` | is true while the button is pressed |
| `while button.value() == 0:` with a short sleep inside, after handling a press | waits for the button to be released, so a long press counts once |
| A program that checks the button once each time round the loop | notices a press only when it reaches the check; it misses a press made while it sleeps |
